case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private federal cause of action allowing private parties to sue for rescission of contracts that allegedly violate the Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Investment Company Act of 1940, Section 47(b), 15 U.S.C. § 80a-46(b) (especially § 47(b)(1)–(3) and the phrase in § 47(b)(2) concerning 'rescission by any party').
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that Section 47(b) does not itself authorize private lawsuits for rescission; it merely supplies a remedial consequence (unenforceability/rescission) that may be applied in enforcement actions brought by the SEC or in cases where an independent, express cause of action exists elsewhere in the ICA. They contend that under this Court’s modern implied-rights jurisprudence (e.g., Sandoval), a private right must be grounded in rights-creating statutory text and structure, and § 47(b) is directed to courts and remedies rather than conferring enforceable rights on private plaintiffs. Petitioners also resist reliance on legislative history and argue that references to TAMA or statutory development cannot overcome the absence of clear, rights-creating language authorizing private suits.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the text and structure of § 47(b)—particularly § 47(b)(2)’s instruction that courts 'shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party' absent specified findings—affirmatively contemplates a party-initiated request for rescission and therefore supplies an express (or at least textually clear) private cause of action for rescission (but not damages). Respondents also contend that this reading fits the provision’s design: § 47(b)(1) establishes contract unenforceability tied to illegality; § 47(b)(2) prescribes when rescission may be sought and when it must not be denied; and § 47(b)(3) resolves remedial follow-on issues like severability and unjust enrichment—features that make sense only if private litigants can invoke the statute in court. They further invoke TAMA and Congress’s post-TAMA amendments as contextual confirmation that Congress meant to allow a limited rescission remedy.
key_precedents: Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis (TAMA), 444 U.S. 11 (1979)
Northwest Airlines, Inc. v. Transport Workers Union of America, 451 U.S. 77 (1981)
Touche Ross & Co. v. Redington, 442 U.S. 560 (1979)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas make the strongest point under Sandoval/Touche Ross: we should not let court-directed remedial language do the work of creating a cause of action, and §36(b) shows Congress knew how to speak clearly when it wanted private enforcement. But the phrase in §47(b)(2) — a court “shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party” — is unusually litigant-invoking, and when read alongside §47(b)(1)’s bilateral “unenforceable by either party” and §47(b)(3)’s severability/unjust-enrichment directions, it functions as a self-contained, party-triggered rescission mechanism that would otherwise be largely surplusage. Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability concern is real, so any opinion I would join must be narrowly limited to equitable rescission (no damages; no freestanding ‘violation’ action) to remain faithful to Sandoval’s clear-statement discipline and the ICA’s overall structure. TAMA does not control under modern doctrine, but it supports the modest inference that Congress’s unlawful-contract “unenforceability” scheme commonly presupposes a limited rescissionary vehicle to make the command operative.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch make the best textual point with the phrase “shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” but I remain persuaded it presupposes a rescission request is already properly before a court through some independently authorized cause of action; it does not itself create that cause. Under Sandoval and Touche Ross, Congress must speak in plaintiff-facing, rights-creating terms to authorize private suit, and §47(b)’s court-directed remedial instructions (“unenforceable,” “shall not deny,” severability/unjust-enrichment guidance) regulate what a court may do once in a case, not who may hale whom into court. Justice Barrett’s reliance on TAMA does not move me because TAMA’s older “fair implication” approach cannot overcome our modern clear-statement discipline, especially given the ICA’s express private remedy in §36(b), which underscores that Congress knew how to confer a private right when it wished. Treating “at the instance of any party” as the authorization clause would invert Sandoval by letting remedy language generate the cause of action, and cabining the result to rescission does not cure the threshold defect: the absence of a textual grant to sue.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch make the best textual point from the other side with §47(b)(2)’s “shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” and I agree the phrase is litigant-oriented. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, that still reads as court-directed remedial constraint once rescission is properly in play (e.g., via an express cause of action, a defensive posture, or government enforcement), not a clear, plaintiff-facing authorization to sue; otherwise we let remedy language do the work of creating a cause of action, which our modern doctrine rejects. Justice Barrett’s reliance on TAMA does not move me because TAMA’s older “fair implication” approach cannot overcome the ICA’s structural signal—especially §36(b)’s express private remedy—that Congress knew how to create private enforcement when it wished, and chose not to do so here. And even a “rescission-only” implied action, as Roberts suggests, would invite broad private enforcement and unsettle contracts in regulated markets without the clear statement Sandoval demands.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas make the strongest point that Sandoval and Touche Ross caution against deriving a cause of action from court-directed remedial language, and I take seriously the structural argument from §36(b)’s express remedy. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively explain that §47(b)(2)’s “shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” read with §47(b)(1)’s bilateral unenforceability and §47(b)(3)’s severability/unjust-enrichment directions, functions as an integrated, party-invoked rescission mechanism that would otherwise be largely inert. Under my pragmatic approach, reading that unusually litigant-facing phrase as mere “discretion limiting” once some other claim exists is too abstract and risks denying meaningful relief to investors when the SEC does not act; a rescission-only holding also answers Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability concern by avoiding damages or free-standing “violation” suits. Sandoval’s clear-statement discipline is respected here because the statute itself supplies the narrow textual hook (“at the instance of any party”) and the remedy’s equitable limits supply a principled stopping point.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas press the best Sandoval/Touche Ross objection—that court-directed remedial language usually cannot do the work of creating a cause of action, and §36(b)’s express remedy cautions against implying more. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that §47(b)(2)’s “shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” read with §47(b)(1)’s bilateral “unenforceable by either party” and §47(b)(3)’s severability/unjust-enrichment directions, is unusually litigant-invoking and functions as an integrated, party-initiated rescission scheme; treating it as mere housekeeping would leave much of the provision with no independent role. On my pragmatic textualist view, Sandoval is satisfied by this specific textual hook so long as we cabin the implied action to equitable rescission (no damages; no freestanding ‘violation’ suit), which also answers much of the §36(b) exclusivity concern. Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability worry underscores why the holding must be narrow, but it does not justify reading “at the instance of any party” as surplusage.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the strongest objection under Sandoval and Touche Ross: court-directed remedial language typically does not, by itself, create a private cause of action, and §36(b)’s express remedy is a meaningful structural cue. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that §47(b)(2)’s “shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” read alongside §47(b)(1)’s bilateral “unenforceable by either party” and §47(b)(3)’s severability/unjust-enrichment instructions, looks like an integrated, party-invoked rescission mechanism that would otherwise be largely inert—this is the kind of specific textual hook Sandoval demands for a narrowly circumscribed implied remedy. Justice Alito’s alternative reading (that §47(b)(2) merely limits discretion once rescission is otherwise properly before the court) does not account for Congress’s decision to specify who may invoke rescission (“any party”) and to legislate the consequences of granting it, which to my mind is more than generic remedial housekeeping. I would therefore adhere to a strictly cabined holding: §47(b) supports only an equitable rescission action (not damages and not a freestanding “violation” suit), which also respects the §36(b) exclusivity concern by keeping implied enforcement at its narrowest textual bounds.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s point that “shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” read alongside §47(b)(1) and (3), looks like a self-contained rescission framework is the strongest argument for Respondent, and I understand the surplusage concern he raises. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, the key question is whether Congress clearly created a private cause of action, and I agree with Justice Alito and Justice Thomas that court-directed remedial commands (“shall not deny”) and status labels (“unenforceable”) typically presuppose an existing vehicle to get into court rather than supply one. Justice Barrett’s reliance on TAMA does not move me because whatever “fair implication” it reflects, our modern doctrine requires a clearer, rights-creating authorization than “at the instance of any party,” especially given the ICA’s express private right in §36(b) signaling Congress knew how to confer one. Cabining the holding to rescission mitigates practical spillover, but it does not solve the threshold problem that we would be letting remedy language generate a cause of action without the clear statement our precedents demand.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas raise the strongest objection under Sandoval and Touche Ross: §47(b)’s court-directed phrasing (“shall not deny”) is not the usual rights-creating, plaintiff-facing language that clearly authorizes suit, and §36(b)’s express private remedy suggests Congress knew how to speak when it wanted private enforcement. But Chief Justice Roberts’s textual point remains persuasive to me: “shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” read with §47(b)(1)’s bilateral unenforceability and §47(b)(3)’s severability/unjust-enrichment directions, most naturally presupposes a party-initiated rescission request rather than merely constraining discretion in some separate, unidentified cause of action. Under an original-public-meaning lens, “at the instance of” is litigant-invoking language, and the alternative reading risks rendering much of §47(b)(2)–(3) largely idle; cabining the implication to equitable rescission (no damages, no freestanding violation action) answers Justice Kavanaugh’s concern by anchoring the holding to the statute’s own remedial limits rather than opening the door to broad private enforcement.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas make the strongest point that, under Sandoval and Touche Ross, court-directed remedial language usually does not itself create a private cause of action, and §36(b)’s express remedy shows Congress can speak clearly when it wants private enforcement. But Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s reading better accounts for the enacted structure: §47(b)(2)’s command that a court “shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” paired with §47(b)(1)’s bilateral unenforceability and §47(b)(3)’s severability/unjust-enrichment directions, operates like a narrow, party-invoked rescission mechanism rather than mere housekeeping once some other claim happens to be in court. Under my fairness- and consequences-focused approach, I would still cabin the holding to equitable rescission (no damages; no freestanding ‘violation’ suits) to respect Sandoval’s clear-statement concerns and address Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability warning while avoiding the practical unfairness of leaving investors without a workable remedy when the SEC does not act. That narrow construction gives operative meaning to “at the instance of any party” without turning §47(b) into broad private enforcement.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 47(b)(2) goes beyond prescribing a remedy in the abstract and instead speaks in party-initiated terms—directing that a court “shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party” absent specified findings—language that most naturally presupposes a litigant’s ability to seek rescission in court. Under Sandoval, we do not invent private enforcement based on statutory purpose, but we also read the text Congress enacted; here, the combination of § 47(b)(1)’s “unenforceable by either party” and § 47(b)(2)–(3)’s detailed rescission framework (including severability and unjust enrichment) is “affirmative evidence” in the statutory text/structure that Congress contemplated a limited private rescission action. This reading is also consistent with Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis, which recognized that when Congress makes certain contracts void or unenforceable, rescission is a traditional and appropriate private remedy—even as damages remain unavailable. A narrow holding recognizing only a rescission cause of action under § 47(b) (and not broader damages or freestanding “violation” suits) best preserves institutional legitimacy by adhering to text and limiting disruptive expansion of implied-rights doctrine.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 47(b) is framed as a remedial consequence—contracts made or performed in violation of the Act are “unenforceable” (§ 47(b)(1)) and courts “shall not deny rescission” absent specified findings (§ 47(b)(2))—but it does not contain the kind of rights-creating, plaintiff-focused language this Court requires to recognize a private cause of action. Under Alexander v. Sandoval, a private right of action must be created by Congress in the statutory text and structure, and court-directed remedial instructions are insufficient to imply private enforcement authority. The ICA’s structure reinforces that conclusion because Congress provided a specific express private right in § 36(b), suggesting that other enforcement mechanisms are primarily administrative or otherwise expressly provided, not implied through § 47(b). TAMA cannot supply what the enacted text lacks, and to the extent any earlier understanding would conflict with Sandoval’s framework, precedent should yield to the statute’s original public meaning as enacted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 47(b) sets out remedial consequences (unenforceability and when courts may grant rescission) but does not contain the kind of rights-creating language that this Court requires to recognize a private federal cause of action. Under Alexander v. Sandoval and related cases like Touche Ross, the existence of a remedy-focused provision—especially one directed to courts—does not authorize private suits absent clear statutory text conferring an enforceable right on a class of plaintiffs. The phrase in § 47(b)(2) about a court not denying “rescission by any party” is best read as limiting a court’s discretion when rescission is otherwise properly before it (e.g., in an SEC action or under another express cause of action), not as an affirmative grant of a new private right to sue. Expanding § 47(b) into a freestanding private rescission action would circumvent Congress’s deliberate choices about who may enforce the ICA and would invite broad, disruptive private litigation with significant practical consequences for regulated markets.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 47(b)’s text and structure most naturally contemplate party-initiated rescission: §47(b)(2) directs that a court “shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party” absent specified findings, language that presupposes a litigant can come to federal court to seek that relief, while §47(b)(3) supplies follow-on rules (severability, unjust enrichment) that would be largely superfluous if rescission could be invoked only defensively. Under Sandoval, the question is statutory intent as reflected in enacted text, and here Congress did more than announce a remedial consequence—it set a judicial standard governing when rescission must be granted, which fits an affirmative, limited private action for rescission (not damages). TAMA supports this limited reading by recognizing that statutory “voidness”/unenforceability language can “fairly impl[y]” a private rescission remedy even when broader damages remedies are not implied; treating §47(b) similarly protects investors and vulnerable shareholders who may lack realistic access to SEC enforcement. Given the ICA’s investor-protection purpose, denying any private rescission action would have significant real-world consequences by leaving unlawful contracts effectively insulated unless and until the SEC acts.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 47(b)’s text and structure read as more than a mere remedial backdrop: §47(b)(1) makes illegal contracts “unenforceable by either party,” while §47(b)(2) instructs that a court “shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party” absent specified findings—language that presupposes a party-initiated request for rescission and supplies a limited private cause of action for that equitable relief. This fits the provision’s internal coherence, because §47(b)(3)’s severability and unjust-enrichment directions address remedial questions that naturally arise when litigants seek rescission, and it would be an odd drafting choice if rescission were only available incidentally in SEC suits or as a defense. Under Sandoval, the touchstone is congressional intent as reflected in enacted text; here the “at the instance of any party” command is the kind of rights-and-remedy linkage that supports recognizing a narrow rescission action, consistent with TAMA’s recognition of a rescission remedy from comparable “void”/unenforceability language. Limiting the remedy to rescission (not damages) also promotes workability and respects the ICA’s overall enforcement design while giving effect to Congress’s specific remedial instructions in §47(b).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The enacted text of §47(b)(2) directs that a court "shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party" absent specified findings, language that presupposes a party-initiated request for rescission and thus supplies an express (or at least textually clear) vehicle for suit limited to that remedy. Read in context with §47(b)(1) (contract "unenforceable by either party") and §47(b)(3) (severability and unjust-enrichment consequences), the provision looks like a self-contained remedial scheme that would be largely inutile if only the SEC could invoke it and no party could seek rescission in court. Under Sandoval, the question is statutory intent as manifested in the words Congress enacted, and the phrase "rescission ... at the instance of any party" is sufficiently rights-conferring for this narrow remedy without resort to legislative history. TAMA supports recognizing rescission (not damages) where Congress uses contract-voiding/rescission language, and §47(b)’s phrasing is, if anything, more explicit than the language at issue there.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under this Court’s modern approach, a private cause of action exists only when Congress clearly creates one in the statutory text and structure. Alexander v. Sandoval and Touche Ross emphasize that remedial or court-directed language is not enough absent rights-creating terms, and ICA §47(b)—even with its references to “rescission by any party” in §47(b)(2)—reads primarily as a remedial rule (unenforceability/rescission) to be applied when a proper enforcement vehicle otherwise exists, not as an affirmative authorization for private suits. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors (TAMA) inferred a rescission remedy from a different statute’s voidness language, but Congress’s choice in §47(b) to frame the provision around unenforceability and judicial standards for granting rescission does not clearly supply the requisite private right of action. As an institutional matter, adhering to Sandoval’s clear-statement discipline promotes administrable, predictable lines and avoids expanding implied causes of action beyond what Congress enacted.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 47(b)(2) provides that a court “shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party” absent specified findings, language that in ordinary usage presupposes party-initiated litigation and thus more naturally reads as authorizing a limited private suit for rescission rather than merely describing remedies available only when the SEC sues. Consistent with Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis, the ICA’s contract-invalidating scheme—here reinforced by §47(b)(1)’s “unenforceable by either party” and §47(b)(3)’s directions on severability and unjust enrichment—fits the traditional inference that Congress contemplated a rescissionary action to effectuate that unenforceability. While Alexander v. Sandoval cautions that private causes of action must be grounded in statutory text and structure (not policy or history), the operative words “rescission … at the instance of any party” supply the requisite textual hook, and recognizing only rescission (not damages) aligns the remedy with the statute’s design. Precedent does not compel the opposite result, and methodological consistency favors reading Congress’s 1980 addition of §47(b)(2) as clarifying, not foreclosing, the TAMA-style rescission remedy.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 47(b)’s text and structure are unusually tailored to party-initiated judicial relief: §47(b)(1) makes illegal contracts “unenforceable by either party,” while §47(b)(2) directs that a court “shall not deny rescission at the instance of any party” absent specified findings—language that most naturally presupposes a litigant’s ability to come to court seeking rescission. Under Sandoval, the touchstone is congressional intent as manifested in enacted text; here, unlike provisions merely supplying a defense, §47(b)(2) and §47(b)(3)’s remedial instructions (severability and unjust enrichment) read as an affirmative, limited rescission cause of action rather than an SEC-only enforcement tool. TAMA reinforces that conclusion by recognizing that parallel “void/un-enforceable” contract language can “fairly imply” a “specific and limited” private remedy of rescission, and the post-TAMA ICA amendments’ focus on rescission mechanics is consistent with Congress contemplating private invocation. Practical consequences also favor this reading: allowing rescission (but not damages) provides a measured investor-protection remedy that promotes procedural fairness without opening the door to broad implied liability.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act of 1940 creates (expressly or by clear implication) a private federal cause of action allowing private parties to seek rescission of contracts that allegedly violate the Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Investment Company Act of 1940, Section 47(b), 15 U.S.C. § 80a-46(b) (especially subsections 47(b)(1)-(3)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that Section 47(b) does not provide private plaintiffs with a federal cause of action for rescission; instead, it supplies a remedial consequence (unenforceability/rescission) that may be invoked only when some other valid cause of action exists (e.g., SEC enforcement or another statutory provision). They rely on the Court’s modern implied-rights framework (e.g., Sandoval) requiring clear rights-creating language and contend that Section 47(b)’s text and structure are court-directed and remedial, not rights-creating. Petitioners also emphasize that recognizing a private rescission remedy would effectively create an end-run around Congress’s limited private-enforcement choices under the ICA and could expand litigation risk beyond what Congress authorized.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the text of Section 47(b), particularly the provision referring to 'rescission by any party' and the accompanying instructions limiting when a court may deny rescission, reflects Congress’s intent to allow parties to illegal ICA contracts to sue for rescission in federal court. They maintain that this is consistent with statutory structure (including provisions addressing severability and restitution/unjust enrichment), and they analogize to the Court’s treatment of similar 'void/unenforceable' language in Transamerica Mortgage Advisors (TAMA). Respondents further contend that the statute’s design—spelling out how courts handle rescission—presupposes a private plaintiff invoking that remedy, and thus supports recognizing a private cause of action at least for rescission (not damages).
key_precedents: Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis (TAMA), 444 U.S. 11 (1979)
Northwest Airlines, Inc. v. Transport Workers Union of America, 451 U.S. 77 (1981)
Touche Ross & Co. v. Redington, 442 U.S. 560 (1979)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s textual point about “rescission at the instance of any party,” reinforced by Justice Sotomayor’s focus on §47(b)(2)–(3)’s restitution/severability instructions, is the strongest case that Congress contemplated party-initiated rescission. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, those features still look like court-directed constraints on equitable discretion once a case is properly before a court through an authorized cause of action; they do not supply the requisite rights-creating, plaintiff-authorizing language to create a freestanding federal claim. Transamerica, as Justice Kagan notes, involved materially different “void” language and predates our modern implied-rights framework, so at most it supports rescission as an available remedy when illegality is established—not §47(b) as an independent jurisdiction-invoking vehicle. Given the ICA’s calibrated scheme with express, narrow private rights (e.g., §36(b)), judicial minimalism and respect for Congress counsel reading §47(b) as remedial/ancillary rather than as silently expanding private federal litigation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s textual emphasis on the phrase “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” is the respondent side’s strongest point because it plainly contemplates a party asking a court for rescission. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, that sort of party-invocation language in a remedial, court-directed provision still does not supply the requisite rights-creating, plaintiff-authorizing text to open federal courthouse doors; it instead constrains the court’s equitable discretion once some valid cause of action is already properly before it. Transamerica, as Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson invoke it, does not alter that conclusion because it construed materially different “void” language in a different doctrinal era, and it cannot override the ICA’s structural choice to provide an express, cabined private action in §36(b) rather than an implied, freestanding rescission suit via §47(b). Reading “any party” to govern rescission when sought within an authorized enforcement vehicle (including defensively or as ancillary relief) gives the phrase effect without judicially creating a new federal cause of action Congress did not clearly enact.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s reliance on the phrase “at the instance of any party,” reinforced by Justice Sotomayor’s point about §47(b)(3)’s restitution/severability directions, is the respondents’ best textual argument because it contemplates a party asking a court for rescission. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, that sort of court-directed remedial instruction still is not the kind of rights-creating, plaintiff-authorizing language that clearly establishes a freestanding federal cause of action; it is more naturally read, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, as constraining equitable discretion once illegality is properly before a court through an authorized vehicle. Transamerica is relevant, as Justice Jackson notes, but it construed materially different “void” language in a different doctrinal era and cannot overcome the ICA’s evident choice to provide express, cabined private remedies elsewhere (notably §36(b)). Given the practical consequences of converting a remedial provision into a new enforcement mechanism, I do not think the text clearly warrants that step.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s Sandoval/Touche Ross point is the hardest for me: we should not transmute court-directed remedial language into a broad, freewheeling private enforcement regime. But §47(b) is unusually party-invocation focused—“a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party”—and, as Justice Barrett emphasizes, §47(b)(3)’s severability/restitution mechanics look like Congress specifying a narrow, self-contained rescission action rather than merely constraining equity after some other claim is in court. I agree with Justice Thomas that the ICA’s express private-right provisions counsel restraint, which is why I would read §47(b) to imply only rescission/restitution (not damages and not generalized enforcement), consistent with Transamerica’s recognition that “void/unenforceable” contract language can carry a limited private unwinding mechanism. On pragmatic grounds, treating §47(b) as purely defensive or SEC-dependent risks leaving investors—especially those most vulnerable—without a realistic path to unwind unlawful contracts, undermining the statute’s protective purpose without any clearer textual alternative.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s point about the phrase “at the instance of any party,” reinforced by Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on §47(b)(3)’s restitution/severability mechanics, is the strongest textual indication that Congress contemplated party-initiated rescission. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, that contemplation is not enough absent rights-creating, plaintiff-authorizing language; §47(b) still reads most naturally as a constraint on a court’s remedial discretion once illegality is properly before it through an authorized cause of action, rather than as a jurisdiction-invoking, freestanding federal claim. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh are also right that converting a remedial provision into an implied cause of action risks upsetting the ICA’s calibrated remedial scheme—especially given Congress’s express, narrow private action in §36(b). Transamerica remains relevant as a signal that rescission can be an available remedy when a contract is unlawful, but its different “void” text and pre-Sandoval context keep it from doing the necessary work of clearly authorizing a new private right of action here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s best point is textual: “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” coupled with §47(b)(3)’s restitution/severability directions, does sound like Congress contemplated a party affirmatively seeking rescission. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, anticipated litigation posture is not the same as rights-creating, plaintiff-authorizing text; these clauses can operate—as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain—as mandatory limits on equitable discretion once a court is properly seized of a case through an authorized cause-of-action and jurisdictional hook (including SEC enforcement or another valid claim where illegality is established). Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Transamerica is the closest precedent, but its different “void” language and pre-Sandoval context, plus the ICA’s calibrated scheme with express private rights like §36(b), make it implausible to infer a new freestanding federal cause of action from §47(b)’s remedial instructions. Giving “any party” effect as governing who may request rescission within an otherwise properly invoked case avoids surplusage without violating separation-of-powers constraints on judicial implication of private rights.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s textual point that “rescission at the instance of any party” contemplates party-initiated litigation is the strongest respondent argument, and Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson reinforce it with §47(b)(3)’s restitution/severability mechanics. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, that kind of court-directed remedial command still is not rights-creating, plaintiff-authorizing language; it can operate as a mandatory remedial rule once illegality is properly before a court via an authorized cause of action (as the Chief emphasizes), including in SEC enforcement or as a defense/counterclaim posture, without implying a new freestanding federal claim. Transamerica is relevant, as Justice Jackson notes, but it interpreted materially different “void” language in a pre-Sandoval implied-rights era, and it cannot overcome the ICA’s structural signal—especially Congress’s express, cabined private action in §36(b)—that broader private enforcement should not be judicially implied. Institutionally and as a matter of workability, recognizing an implied §47(b) private action would expand federal litigation in a way Congress did not clearly authorize, so I remain with Petitioner.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s Sandoval/Touche Ross objection is the strongest: court-directed remedial language often does not itself create a cause of action, and the ICA’s express private-right choices (as Justice Thomas stresses) counsel caution. But §47(b)(2)’s phrase “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” read in ordinary legal usage, contemplates a party-initiated request and is awkward to recharacterize as purely defensive or merely a constraint that springs to life only after some other authorized claim is already in court. Justice Thomas is right that we should not infer a broad enforcement regime; the better textual fit is a narrow, contract-focused rescission/restitution mechanism bounded by §47(b)(3), which avoids turning §47(b) into a general private right to enforce the ICA while still giving “at the instance of any party” independent operative effect. Transamerica, though pre-Sandoval and involving different “void” language, remains relevant in showing that Congress’s use of unenforceability/voidness concepts can carry with it a limited rescission action rather than an open-ended implied right.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Sandoval/Touche Ross concern—that §47(b)’s court-directed phrasing can operate only once some other valid cause of action is properly before a court—is the most serious constraint on my view, because we should not invent federal claims from remedial language alone. But Justice Barrett’s textual point remains dispositive for me: “a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” coupled with §47(b)(2)–(3)’s mandatory restitution/severability mechanics, reads as Congress specifying a party-invocable rescission pathway that would be oddly surplus if it could never be affirmatively sought. Justice Thomas’s structural argument about Congress’s express private-right choices elsewhere is important, yet I think it is accommodated by recognizing only a narrow rescission/restitution remedy (not damages), which respects institutional limits while giving practical effect to Congress’s declaration that illegal contracts are “unenforceable by either party.” Transamerica’s treatment of void/unenforceable contract language—though pre-Sandoval and not a blank check—still supports the limited inference that Congress can authorize rescission implicitly when it writes in contract-unwinding terms, and I do not read Sandoval as requiring us to ignore this unusually party-invocation-focused text.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under our modern implied-rights framework, we ask whether Congress clearly created a private cause of action, and remedial language alone is not enough. Section 47(b) speaks in court-directed, remedial terms—rendering certain contracts “unenforceable” and describing when “a court may not deny rescission,” 15 U.S.C. §80a-46(b)(1)-(2)—but it does not use the sort of rights-creating language that Sandoval requires to infer a private federal cause of action. TAMA is distinguishable because it construed different statutory text (§215 of the IAA) in a different era of implied-rights analysis, and reading §47(b) to authorize private suits risks expanding private enforcement beyond the ICA’s carefully cabined scheme, contrary to Northwest Airlines and Touche Ross. A narrow holding preserving institutional legitimacy is to treat §47(b) as specifying a remedy (rescission/unenforceability) available only when some other valid cause of action is properly before the court (e.g., SEC enforcement), rather than as an independent private right of action.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under a strict textualist approach, ICA §47(b) sets out a remedial consequence (a contract is “unenforceable” and may be rescinded) but does not itself create a private federal cause of action, because it lacks the kind of rights-creating language focused on protected persons that Sandoval and Touche Ross require for implied private enforcement. The provision is written as a rule of decision for courts (“a court may not deny rescission unless…”) and can operate defensively or within an otherwise valid action (including SEC enforcement), without authorizing a new freestanding federal suit. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors (TAMA) does not compel the opposite result because it inferred a limited remedy from materially different statutory language and, in any event, modern implied-rights doctrine demands clearer congressional authorization than §47(b) supplies. Given the ICA’s structure—where Congress expressly created narrow private actions in §36(b) (and elsewhere) but otherwise vested enforcement in the SEC—recognizing a broad private rescission action under §47(b) would contradict the statute’s text and design.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Alexander v. Sandoval and this Court’s modern implied-rights cases, a private federal cause of action must be grounded in clear rights-creating language, not merely in remedial or court-directed instructions. ICA §47(b)(1)–(3) speaks in terms of contract unenforceability and when “a court may not deny rescission,” but it does not identify a protected class, confer an individual entitlement, or otherwise supply the sort of rights-creating language that Sandoval and Touche Ross require. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors (TAMA) does not compel the opposite result because it turned on the particular statutory text of IAA §215(b) and was decided in a different era of implied-rights doctrine; in any event, recognizing a broad private rescission action here would risk end-running Congress’s calibrated enforcement scheme under the ICA with substantial practical litigation consequences.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 47(b) goes beyond merely describing a consequence of illegality: it directs that a court “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” absent specified findings, and §47(b)(3) supplies remedial details (severability and restitution/unjust enrichment) that make sense only if parties can affirmatively invoke rescission in court, not merely as a defensive theory. Under Sandoval, the touchstone is congressional intent as reflected in text and structure; here, the statute’s rights-remedy pairing (“rescission by any party” plus limits on judicial discretion) is a sufficiently clear implication of a limited private cause of action for rescission, even if not for damages. This reading aligns with Transamerica Mortgage Advisors (TAMA), which treated analogous “void”/unenforceable-contract language as implying a private rescission remedy, and it promotes fairness and investor protection—the core ICA purpose—especially for shareholders least able to rely on sporadic SEC enforcement.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 47(b) reads as a remedial rule of decision—making certain ICA-tainted contracts “unenforceable by either party” and describing when “a court” may deny “rescission by any party”—but it does not speak in rights-creating terms or identify who may sue, which is the touchstone under Alexander v. Sandoval for recognizing a private federal cause of action. Unlike the provision in Transamerica Mortgage Advisors (TAMA) that the Court found to “fairly imply” a limited rescission remedy based on specific statutory language, Section 47(b)’s court-directed and remedial phrasing is more naturally understood to operate when a plaintiff is properly in court under some other cause of action (including SEC enforcement or state-law contract/equity claims), not to create a new freestanding federal claim. The ICA’s structure reinforces that conclusion: when Congress wanted private enforcement it did so expressly (e.g., §§ 36(b), 30(h)), and we should be wary of letting §47(b) become an end-run around those calibrated choices, consistent with Touche Ross and Northwest Airlines. Interpreting §47(b) to supply rescission only as a consequence once a violation is established through an authorized vehicle preserves statutory coherence and avoids substantial workability concerns from broad implied litigation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 47(b) supplies a rule of contractual unenforceability and a remedial consequence (including when a court may deny rescission), but it does not itself create a private federal cause of action; under Alexander v. Sandoval, we do not infer private suits absent clear rights-creating language directed to private plaintiffs. The text of §47(b)(1)–(3) is largely court-directed and remedial ("unenforceable," "a court may not deny rescission unless"), and the ICA’s structure shows Congress knew how to authorize private enforcement when it wished (e.g., §§30(h), 36(b)), counseling against implying additional causes of action. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors (TAMA) does not compel a different result here because Sandoval’s stricter framework requires a clearer textual indication of a privately enforceable right than §47(b) provides, and any rescission effect can still operate defensively or ancillary to another valid cause of action. Given the separation-of-powers concerns inherent in judicially creating new federal causes of action, the better reading is that §47(b) prescribes consequences when illegality is properly before a court, not a freestanding private suit.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Sandoval and Touche Ross, the question is whether Congress clearly created a private cause of action in the statutory text and structure, and Section 47(b) reads as a remedial provision governing enforceability and the availability of rescission once a violation is properly before a court, not as rights-creating language authorizing private plaintiffs to sue. The ICA’s express private-enforcement choices elsewhere (e.g., its limited express private rights) counsel against inferring an additional, freestanding rescission cause of action from Section 47(b), consistent with Northwest Airlines’ reluctance to imply remedies where Congress has specified enforcement mechanisms. Transamerica (TAMA) does not compel the opposite result because it predates Sandoval’s clear-statement approach and turned on materially different “void” language in a different statute, whereas 47(b)’s court-directed limitations on when rescission may be denied can operate as a defense or remedial rule without implying a new federal claim. Given precedent, history, and practical workability, recognizing a private rescission cause of action here would risk expanding litigation beyond what Congress clearly authorized.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 47(b)’s text goes beyond merely stating a remedial consequence and instead presupposes an action for rescission: it directs that, once a violating contract has been performed, “a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” absent specified equitable findings, and it separately addresses severability and unjust enrichment in §47(b)(2)–(3). Read in context, that court-directed, party-invoking language is best understood to authorize a limited private suit for rescission by parties to the unlawful contract, consistent with the original public meaning of “unenforceable by either party” in §47(b)(1). This construction also fits this Court’s treatment of analogous “void”/unenforceability language in Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis, which recognized a limited private right to seek rescission while declining to infer broader remedies, and it is not displaced by Sandoval because the cause of action is grounded in the statute’s own remedial instruction tied to “any party” seeking rescission. Precedent cautions against expanding implied rights beyond what Congress provided, but recognizing only rescission (not damages) tracks the statute’s carefully cabined remedial scheme.

That structure resembles the statutory “void” language this Court treated as authorizing a limited private rescission remedy in Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis (TAMA), even if Sandoval cautions against implying broad private enforcement absent clear congressional intent; here, Congress wrote detailed, court-administered rescission instructions that would have little practical work if no party could invoke them. Recognizing only a rescission cause of action (not damages) respects the statute’s remedial limits and serves procedural fairness by allowing investors/contracting parties to unwind unlawful arrangements without expanding liability beyond what § 47(b) specifies.
